cse-1994-b-39-a.approach: Compare the control-transfer discipline: a subroutine always starts at its entry and finishes before returning, whereas a coroutine suspends and later resumes where it left off.

steps.title: Subroutine behaviour
steps.body: A subroutine is entered at a single entry point every time it is called; it runs to completion and then returns to its caller. The caller and callee are in a **master-slave** relation.

steps.title: Coroutine behaviour
steps.body: A coroutine can **suspend** itself (e.g. `resume` / `yield`) and pass control to another coroutine; when resumed, it continues from the point of suspension with its local state preserved. Coroutines are **symmetric** peers, so each needs its own preserved activation (often its own stack).

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Because a coroutine has multiple entry (resume) points and survives across transfers, it is not just another name for a subroutine. The statement is **False**.

answer.value: False — a coroutine resumes from where it last suspended (multiple entry points, preserved state); a subroutine always restarts at its entry and runs to completion.

pitfalls: A subroutine is a special case of a coroutine, not the other way round.
cse-1994-b-39-a.verification: Generators in Python/C# (`yield`) are coroutines: calling them twice continues execution instead of restarting it — impossible for an ordinary subroutine.

cse-1994-b-39-b.approach: Recall what pass 1 of a two-pass assembler must compute — the symbol table — and what it needs for that: the length of every instruction, which comes from the machine opcode table (MOT).

steps.title: Job of pass 1
steps.body: Pass 1 assigns an address to every label: it walks the source, keeps a **location counter (LC)** and enters each label with the current LC value into the symbol table.

steps.title: Why the MOT is needed in pass 1
steps.body: To advance the LC past a machine instruction, pass 1 must know that instruction's **length**, and the length (plus validity of the mnemonic) is stored in the machine opcode table. So pass 1 looks up every mnemonic in the MOT (pseudo-ops are looked up in the POT).

steps.title: Pass 2
steps.body: Pass 2 uses the MOT again, this time for the binary opcode and format, and the symbol table for operand addresses. Hence the MOT is used in **both** passes, in particular in the first. The statement is **True**.

answer.value: True — pass 1 consults the machine opcode table to get each instruction's length so it can update the location counter and build the symbol table.

pitfalls: Thinking the MOT is used only in pass 2 for code generation — pass 1 needs instruction lengths from it.
cse-1994-b-39-b.verification: Standard (Donovan/IBM 360) two-pass design: pass 1 tables = MOT (lengths), POT, ST, LT; pass 2 = MOT (opcodes), POT, ST, BT.

cse-1994-b-40-a.approach: A macro is expanded at assembly time and can generate different code for different arguments; a subroutine is one fixed piece of code executed at run time. Find a macro use that a run-time call cannot reproduce.

steps.title: What a macro can do
steps.body: A macro is text substitution at **assembly time**. Its parameters can be anything textual: an opcode, a register name, a label, a data definition, and with conditional assembly (`AIF`, `IF`) it can emit different instructions for different arguments.

steps.title: What a subroutine cannot do
steps.body: A subroutine is a single block of machine code; it can only receive **run-time values** as parameters. It cannot change the opcode it executes, declare data or labels at the call site, or vary its own code per call. A call also changes the return-address register/stack, which matters in code that must not disturb it (e.g. interrupt prologues).

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Example: `MACRO INCR &R` expanding to `ADD &R,=F'1'` with a different register per call, or a macro that defines a data area. No subroutine can replace these, so a subroutine **cannot always** replace a macro. The statement is **True**.

answer.value: True — macros are expanded at assembly time and can generate different instructions, labels or data per call; a subroutine is fixed code receiving only run-time values.

pitfalls: The reverse is also not always possible, but the question asks only about subroutine replacing macro.
cse-1994-b-40-a.verification: A single counter-example (a macro whose parameter is an opcode or register) suffices to show "cannot always".

cse-1994-b-40-b.approach: An external symbol is defined in another, separately assembled module, so the assembler has no way to know its address; resolution is the linker/loader's job.

steps.title: What EXTERN means
steps.body: Declaring a symbol `EXTRN` / `extern` says: this symbol is **used here but defined in some other module**.

steps.title: What the assembler does
steps.body: The assembler assembles one module at a time. For an external symbol it emits a placeholder (usually 0) in the instruction and records the reference in the object module's **external reference / relocation list**; it does not assign any address.

steps.title: Who assigns the address
steps.body: The **linker (or linking loader)** combines modules, finds the module that defines the symbol (its `ENTRY`/`PUBLIC` definition), and patches every reference with the final address. So the statement is **False**.

answer.value: False — the assembler only records the external reference; the linker/loader resolves its address when modules are combined.

pitfalls: Confusing an external symbol with a relocatable internal one: internal symbols get module-relative addresses from the assembler, external ones get none.
cse-1994-b-40-b.verification: In an ELF object file, an `extern` reference appears as an undefined symbol (`U` in `nm`) with a relocation entry — no address.

cse-1994-b-41-a.approach: Decide which statement can actually be proved without knowing the digits of pi. Semi-deciding membership is easy by scanning pi's expansion; regularity or decidability would require knowledge of pi nobody has. Also note regular ⇒ recursive ⇒ r.e., so a single correct option can only be (ii).

steps.title: S is r.e. — option (ii)
steps.body: Pi is computable, so a TM can generate its decimal digits one by one. Whenever it sees a run of 5's bounded by a non-5 digit on **both** sides, it outputs the run length $x$. Every $x \in S$ is eventually output, so $S$ is enumerated: $S$ is **recursively enumerable**.

steps.title: Recursive / regular are not provable
steps.body: To decide $x \notin S$ we would have to know that no maximal block of exactly $x$ fives ever occurs in the infinite expansion. Nothing about pi's digits is known that guarantees this, and with the **maximal** condition $S$ need not be an initial segment of $\mathbb{N}$ or all of $\mathbb{N}$, so the usual "S is $\mathbb{N}$ or $\{1,\dots,k\}$, hence regular" argument does not apply. So (i) and (iv) cannot be asserted.

steps.title: Rule out by containment
steps.body: Regular $\subset$ recursive $\subset$ r.e. If (i) were true, (ii) and (iv) would be true as well, contradicting a single correct option; similarly (iv) implies (ii). (iii) contradicts the proof of (ii). The only statement that is true is **(ii)**.

optionAnalysis.reason: (i) Regularity would follow only if $S$ were $\mathbb{N}$ or an initial segment, which holds for non-maximal blocks; for maximal blocks it is unproven — and it would also make (ii) and (iv) true.
(ii) Enumerate pi's digits and output the length of every maximal run of 5's found; this enumerates exactly $S$.
(iii) Contradicted by the enumeration procedure for (ii).
(iv) Deciding non-membership needs a guarantee about all of pi's infinitely many digits; not provable, and it would make (ii) true too.

pitfalls: Dropping the word "maximal": for non-maximal blocks $S$ is downward closed, hence $\mathbb{N}$ or $\{0..k\}$, hence regular.
Forgetting regular ⇒ recursive ⇒ r.e. when only one option may be chosen.
cse-1994-b-41-a.verification: The containment argument alone fixes the single answer: any of (i)/(iv) true forces (ii) true, so the unique true statement must be (ii).

cse-1994-b-41-b.approach: Give a counter-example: choose $L_1 = \Sigma^*$, which absorbs any $L_2$ in the union, so $L_1 \cup L_2$ is regular whatever $L_2$ is.

steps.title: Pick the languages
steps.body: Let $\Sigma = \{a, b\}$, $L_1 = \Sigma^*$ (regular) and $L_2 = \{a^n b^n \mid n \ge 0\}$ (not regular, by the pumping lemma).

steps.title: Compute the union
steps.body: Since $L_2 \subseteq \Sigma^*$, $L_1 \cup L_2 = \Sigma^*$, which is regular.

steps.title: Conclude
steps.body: Both hypotheses hold, yet $L_2$ is not regular. Hence $L_2$ is **not always** regular. (Regular languages are not closed under "set difference from a union": $L_2$ is only guaranteed to lie between $(L_1\cup L_2) - L_1$ and $L_1 \cup L_2$.)

answer.value: No. Counter-example: $L_1 = \Sigma^*$, $L_2 = \{a^n b^n\}$; $L_1 \cup L_2 = \Sigma^*$ is regular but $L_2$ is not.

pitfalls: Arguing $L_2 = (L_1 \cup L_2) - L_1$ — that is only true when $L_1 \cap L_2 = \emptyset$.
cse-1994-b-41-b.verification: If additionally $L_1 \cap L_2 = \emptyset$, then $L_2 = (L_1\cup L_2)\cap \overline{L_1}$ would be regular — the counter-example works precisely because $L_2 \subseteq L_1$.

cse-1994-b-42.approach: Count the two kinds of production uses separately: each $A \to BC$ adds one non-terminal, and each $A \to a$ turns one non-terminal into a terminal.

steps.title: Terminal productions
steps.body: Every symbol of $w$ comes from exactly one use of a rule $A \to a$, so there are exactly $l$ such steps.

steps.title: Binary productions
steps.body: Start with 1 non-terminal ($S$). Each $A \to BC$ step increases the number of non-terminals by $1$; a terminal step decreases it by 1. To end up with $l$ non-terminals to be turned into terminals we need $l - 1$ binary steps (the parse tree's internal binary nodes form a full binary tree with $l$ leaves, which has $l-1$ internal nodes).

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $$\underbrace{(l-1)}_{A\to BC} + \underbrace{l}_{A\to a} = 2l - 1$$ So every derivation of $w$ (with $l \ge 1$) has exactly $2l-1$ steps.

answer.value: Exactly $2l - 1$ steps ($l-1$ uses of $A \to BC$ and $l$ uses of $A \to a$).

pitfalls: Answering $l$ or $2l$: forgetting that a full binary tree with $l$ leaves has $l-1$ internal nodes.
cse-1994-b-42.verification: With $S \to AB$, $A \to a$, $B \to b$: $w = ab$, $l = 2$: $S \Rightarrow AB \Rightarrow aB \Rightarrow ab$ — 3 steps $= 2(2)-1$.

cse-1994-b-43.approach: The stack holds at most one frame per active call; find the frame size and the deepest chain of simultaneously active calls of `fib(n)`.
cse-1994-b-43.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Stack size | 64 bytes |
| Per call | return address (2 B) + parameter n (2 B) |

steps.title: Frame size
steps.body: Each call pushes its return address and the parameter: $2 + 2 = 4$ bytes. So the stack can hold $\dfrac{64}{4} = 16$ frames at once.

steps.title: Deepest call chain
steps.body: Calls are evaluated left first: `fib(n)` calls `fib(n-1)`, which calls `fib(n-2)`, …, down to `fib(1)` (a base case). The longest chain of simultaneously active calls is `fib(n), fib(n-1), …, fib(1)`: **$n$ frames**. The call `fib(n-2)` happens only after `fib(n-1)` has returned, so it never deepens the stack beyond this.

scene.caption: Deepest point for n = 16: 16 frames × 4 B = 64 B

steps.title: Maximum n
steps.body: Need $4n \le 64 \Rightarrow n \le 16$. For $n = 16$ the stack is exactly full at the bottom of the chain; for $n = 17$ it needs 68 bytes and overflows. Maximum $n = $ **16**.

pitfalls: Counting all $O(\phi^n)$ calls instead of only the active ones on the stack.
Assuming `fib(0)` lies one level deeper: `fib(2)` calls `fib(0)` at the same depth as `fib(1)`.
cse-1994-b-43.verification: If the caller of `fib(n)` (main program) also used the same stack, or a local for the result were stored, the answer would drop to 15 — the question says only return address and parameter are pushed.

cse-1994-b-44-i.approach: Under static scoping a free variable is bound by the textually enclosing declaration, which never changes — so every call of `two` reads the global `r`.

steps.title: Resolve r in two
steps.body: Procedure `two` is declared at the outer level of `main`, so its only enclosing scope is `main`. The free `r` in `write(r)` therefore always means the **global** `r` of `main`, no matter who calls `two`.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body:
`r := 2` sets global `r = 2`.

1. `two` → prints global `r` = **2**.
2. `one` declares its own local `r`, sets it to 5, calls `two` → `two` still reads the global `r` = **2**.
3. `two` → **2**.

steps.title: Output
steps.body: The program prints **2 2 2**. The assignment `r := 5` in `one` changes only `one`'s local `r`, which is invisible to `two` under static scoping.

pitfalls: Thinking `r := 5` inside `one` modifies the global `r` — it targets `one`'s own local.
cse-1994-b-44-i.verification: Static link of `two`'s frame always points to `main`'s frame, whose `r` is 2 throughout.

cse-1994-b-44-ii.approach: Under dynamic scoping a free variable is bound by the most recent active declaration on the call stack, so the answer depends on who called `two`.

steps.title: Rule
steps.body: With dynamic scoping, `two` looks up `r` by walking the **call chain** back from `two` and uses the first activation that declares `r`.

steps.title: Trace
steps.body:
`r := 2` sets main's `r = 2`.

1. `main → two`: nearest `r` is main's → **2**.
2. `main → one → two`: `one` declared `r` and set it to 5; that is the nearest `r` → **5**.
3. `main → two`: `one` has returned, nearest `r` is main's → **2**.

scene.caption: Second call of two: nearest r on the stack is one's r = 5

steps.title: Output
steps.body: The program prints **2 5 2**.

answer.value: 2 5 2 — the call from `one` sees `one`'s local `r = 5`; the two calls from `main` see `r = 2`.

pitfalls: Keeping 5 for the third call: `one`'s activation (and its `r`) is gone once `one` returns.
cse-1994-b-44-ii.verification: Compare with static scoping (2 2 2): only the call made from inside `one` differs, as expected.

cse-1994-b-45.approach: Give each E and T an attribute `place` (the memory address holding its value). Since the machine has one register, every addition is LOAD-ADD-STORE into a fresh temporary, and the assignment is LOAD-STORE.

steps.title: Attributes and helpers
steps.body: `E.place`, `T.place` = address holding the value. `newtemp()` returns a fresh temporary location; `emit(…)` appends an instruction.

steps.title: Translation scheme
steps.body:
| Production | Semantic action |
|---|---|
| $A \to id := E$ | `emit(LOAD E.place); emit(STORE id.place)` |
| $E \to E_1 + T$ | `E.place := newtemp(); emit(LOAD E1.place); emit(ADD T.place); emit(STORE E.place)` |
| $E \to T$ | `E.place := T.place` |
| $T \to (E)$ | `T.place := E.place` |
| $T \to id$ | `T.place := id.place` |

steps.title: Example: x := a + (b + c)
steps.body: Bottom-up: inner $b + c$ gives `LOAD b; ADD c; STORE t1`; outer $a + t1$ gives `LOAD a; ADD t1; STORE t2`; assignment gives `LOAD t2; STORE x`.

steps.title: Optional optimisation
steps.body: Keeping a flag "value already in register" lets $E \to E_1 + T$ skip `LOAD` when $E_1$ was just computed, and $A \to id := E$ skip `LOAD t`; this gives `LOAD b; ADD c; STORE t1; LOAD a; ADD t1; STORE x`. The basic scheme above is already correct.

answer.value: Use attribute `place`: $T \to id$: T.place = id; $T \to (E)$: T.place = E.place; $E \to T$: E.place = T.place; $E \to E_1 + T$: t = newtemp, emit LOAD E1.place, ADD T.place, STORE t, E.place = t; $A \to id := E$: emit LOAD E.place, STORE id.

pitfalls: Emitting ADD without first loading $E_1$ — the single register may hold some other value.
Not storing the sum: the register is overwritten by the next LOAD.
cse-1994-b-45.verification: Running the example code with a=1, b=2, c=3 leaves x = 6.

cse-1994-b-46-a.approach: Exchange argument: some maximum independent set always contains any given leaf (swap its parent out for it). So repeatedly take leaves of what remains, and keep a leaf unless one of its already-processed neighbours (its children) was taken.

steps.title: Greedy choice: leaves
steps.body: Let $u$ be a leaf with parent $p$. If an optimal set $I^*$ omits $u$, it must contain $p$ (else add $u$). Then $I^* - \{p\} + \{u\}$ is still independent and the same size. So taking a leaf is always safe.

steps.title: Completed algorithm
Why the second condition
steps.body: Removing $u$ from $V$ makes its parent a leaf later. When the parent $v$ is selected, its processed neighbours are its children; if any child is in $I$, $v$ is skipped (it is the "parent removed" in the exchange argument), otherwise it is added. This is exactly the leaf-greedy, so the output is a **maximum** independent set.

answer.value: First blank: $u$ is a leaf (degree ≤ 1) in the remaining forest $V$. Second blank: no neighbour of $u$ is already in $I$ (equivalently, none of its children was selected).

pitfalls: Choosing "u has maximum/minimum degree" in the original tree — degree must be measured in what remains of $V$.
cse-1994-b-46-a.verification: Path a–b–c–d: leaves a (take), d (take), then b (neighbour a in I, skip), c (neighbour d in I, skip) → {a, d}, size 2 = optimum for $P_4$.

cse-1994-b-46-b.approach: Each vertex is selected and tested once; with leaves kept in a queue and degree counters, every step is O(1) amortised over the edges.

steps.title: Implementation
steps.body: Keep `deg[v]` (degree in remaining $V$), a queue of current leaves, and a boolean `inI[v]`. Initialise in $O(n)$.

steps.title: Cost per vertex
steps.body: Dequeue a leaf $u$ ($O(1)$). Test "some neighbour in $I$" and decrement `deg` of its neighbours, enqueuing those that become leaves — $O(\deg(u))$. Summed over all vertices: $\sum \deg(u) = 2(n-1)$.

steps.title: Total
steps.body: $O(n) + O(2(n-1)) = O(n)$. (A naive scan of $V$ to find a leaf each time would cost $O(n^2)$.)

answer.value: $O(n)$ for a tree with $n$ vertices (leaves kept in a queue; total work proportional to $n + 2(n-1)$).

pitfalls: Quoting $O(n^2)$ by assuming every selection scans all of $V$ — that is an implementation choice, not inherent.
cse-1994-b-46-b.verification: This is a reverse BFS / post-order traversal of the tree, which is linear.

cse-1994-b-47.approach: Two pointers from both ends of the sorted array: a too-small sum can only be fixed by moving the left pointer right, a too-large sum only by moving the right pointer left. Each step discards one index, so at most n steps.

steps.title: Algorithm
Correctness
steps.body: If $A[i] + A[j] < x$, then $A[i] + A[k] \le A[i] + A[j] < x$ for every $k \le j$, so index $i$ can pair with nothing left: discard it. Symmetrically, if $A[i] + A[j] > x$, index $j$ can pair with nothing $\ge i$: discard it. No valid pair is ever skipped.

steps.title: Time
steps.body: Each iteration increases $i$ or decreases $j$, so $j - i$ drops by 1 each time: at most $n$ iterations, $O(n)$ time and $O(1)$ space.

answer.value: Two pointers: i := 1, j := n; while i ≤ j: if A[i]+A[j] = x report (i, j); else if the sum < x then i := i+1 else j := j−1. O(n).

pitfalls: Using binary search per element — correct but $O(n \log n)$, not linear.

cse-1994-b-48.approach: A queue→stack transfer reverses order. Doing it once puts the front at the bottom; transferring back to the queue and then to the stack again reverses twice more, leaving the front on top — 3n operations, no extra storage.

animation.caption: Example with n = 3; a1 is the front

steps.title: Q → S
steps.body: Repeat $n$ times: `Push(S, Delete(Q))`. Now S holds $a_1$ at the bottom and $a_n$ on top — reversed.

steps.title: S → Q
steps.body: Repeat $n$ times: `Insert(Q, Pop(S))`. Q is now $a_n, \dots, a_1$ from front to rear.

scene.caption: After pass 2: queue front is a3

steps.title: Q → S again
steps.body: Repeat $n$ times: `Push(S, Delete(Q))`. $a_n$ goes in first (bottom) and $a_1$ last, so $a_1$ — the original front — is on **top**, with the rest in order beneath it.

scene.caption: After pass 3: top is a1 (original front)

steps.title: Cost
steps.body: $3n$ operations, i.e. $O(n)$ time; only a loop counter (to count $n$, or an emptiness test) is needed — $O(1)$ extra storage.

answer.value: Delete all n items from Q pushing each on S; pop all from S inserting each into Q; then delete all from Q pushing each on S. Front ends on top; 3n operations, O(1) extra space.

pitfalls: Stopping after one transfer: the front ends at the bottom of the stack.
cse-1994-b-48.verification: Traced with a1, a2, a3 above: final stack top-to-bottom a1, a2, a3 — same order as the original queue front-to-rear.

cse-1994-b-49-a.approach: Draw an edge Si → Sj whenever Sj must wait for Si: data dependences (read-after-write, write-after-read, write-after-write on n, i, a(i)) and the control dependence on the test in S3. Keep only non-redundant edges.

steps.title: Dependences
steps.body:
- $S_1 \to S_3$, $S_2 \to S_3$: $S_3$ reads n and i.
- $S_3 \to S_4$: $S_4$ runs only if the test fails (control); also $S_2 \to S_4$ (reads i).
- $S_4 \to S_5$: $S_5$ overwrites i, which $S_4$ reads (anti-dependence).
- $S_5 \to S_6$: $S_6$ reads the new i; $S_4 \to S_6$: reads a(i); $S_3 \to S_6$: control.

steps.title: Remove transitive edges
steps.body: $S_2 \to S_4$ is implied by $S_2 \to S_3 \to S_4$; $S_4 \to S_6$ and $S_3 \to S_6$ by $S_3 \to S_4 \to S_5 \to S_6$. The graph is: $S_1$ and $S_2$ in parallel, both $\to S_3 \to S_4 \to S_5 \to S_6$.

scene.caption: S1 and S2 are independent; everything else is a chain

answer.value: Edges $S_1 \to S_3$, $S_2 \to S_3$, $S_3 \to S_4$, $S_4 \to S_5$, $S_5 \to S_6$ (implied edges $S_2 \to S_4$, $S_3 \to S_6$, $S_4 \to S_6$ may also be drawn). Only $S_1$ and $S_2$ can run concurrently.

pitfalls: Letting $S_5$ run in parallel with $S_4$: $S_5$ changes i, which $S_4$ uses as index and value.
Treating `goto next` as a loop — it is a forward jump, so the code has no cycle.
cse-1994-b-49-a.verification: Any topological order of the graph (e.g. S2, S1, S3, S4, S5, S6) produces the same values as the sequential program.

cse-1994-b-49-b.approach: A precedence graph is expressible with parbegin/parend alone iff it is series-parallel (properly nested). Here it is a parallel pair followed by a chain.

steps.title: Shape of the graph
steps.body: From (a): $S_1 \parallel S_2$, then $S_3 \to S_4 \to S_5 \to S_6$ in sequence. A fork into $S_1, S_2$ followed by one join before $S_3$ is properly nested.

steps.title: Concurrent program
steps.body:
```
begin
    parbegin S1; S2 parend;
    S3; S4; S5; S6
end
```
(The `goto next` in $S_3$ simply skips $S_4, S_5$ inside the sequential part.)

steps.title: Conclusion
steps.body: **Yes** — the graph is series-parallel, so parbegin-parend suffices. (Graphs such as $S_1\to S_3$, $S_1\to S_4$, $S_2\to S_4$ with no common join would need semaphores.)

answer.value: Yes: `parbegin S1; S2 parend; S3; S4; S5; S6`.

pitfalls: Assuming every precedence graph can be written with parbegin/parend — only properly nested (series-parallel) ones can.
cse-1994-b-49-b.verification: The program enforces exactly the edges of (a): S3 starts after both S1 and S2 end, and the rest is sequential.

cse-1994-b-50-a.approach: With multi-instance resources a cycle is not enough; run the deadlock-detection (reduction) algorithm: repeatedly satisfy any process whose request fits in Available and reclaim its allocation.

steps.title: Read the graph
steps.body: An arrow from an instance dot to a process is an **allocation**; an arrow from a process to a box is a **request**. Reading every arrow of the figure gives the matrices in the table above.

steps.title: Verdict
steps.body: Every process can finish, so the graph reduces completely: the system is **not deadlocked**, even though the graph contains cycles (e.g. P1 → T1 → P0 → T2 → P1).

answer.value: No — the graph is completely reducible (P2, P0, P1, P3 can finish in that order), so there is no deadlock.

pitfalls: Declaring deadlock because of a cycle: with several instances per resource a cycle is necessary but not sufficient.
cse-1994-b-50-a.verification: Final Available (2,3,2) equals the total instances, confirming all allocations were reclaimed.

cse-1994-b-50-b.approach: Run the safety algorithm on the current requests: start from Available, pick any process whose outstanding request fits, let it finish and release its allocation, repeat.

steps.title: Read the graph
steps.body: An arrow from an instance dot to a process is an **allocation**; an arrow from a process to a box is a **request**. Reading every arrow of the figure gives the matrices in the table above.

steps.title: P2 first
steps.body: Only P2's request (0,0,1) fits in (0,0,1) (P0 needs a T2, P1 a T1, P3 a T1 and two T2). P2 finishes and releases (0,1,0): Available $= (0,1,1)$.

steps.title: Then P0
steps.body: P0 requests (0,1,1) ≤ (0,1,1). It finishes and releases (1,0,1): Available $= (1,1,2)$.

steps.title: Then P1 and P3
steps.body: P1 requests (1,0,0) ≤ (1,1,2) → releases (1,1,0): Available $= (2,2,2)$. P3 requests (1,2,0) ≤ (2,2,2) → releases (0,1,0): Available $= (2,3,2)$.

answer.value: Safe sequence: P2 → P0 → P1 → P3 (the only one: P2 must go first, then P0, and P3 needs two T2 instances so it must wait for P1).

pitfalls: Starting with P1 or P3: Available has no free T1 or T2 at the start.
cse-1994-b-50-b.verification: Uniqueness check: at Available (0,0,1) only P2 fits; at (0,1,1) only P0; at (1,1,2) P1 fits but P3 does not (needs 2 × T2, only 1 free); at (2,2,2) P3 fits. Final Available (2,3,2) equals the totals.
